title.narrative: ECHO Lebanon led by AVSI - Back to the Future

description.narrative: BTF VI adopts a nexus approach by integrating humanitarian action with development strategies. This reflects the commitment to reduce underlying vulnerabilities and risks while creating sustainable pathways for the targeted population. It empowers communities, engages the most vulnerable, creates supportive environments, builds capacities and strengthens coping mechanisms, while also transferring ownership. On the other hand, BTF VI creates opportunities for bridging humanitarian aid with developmental efforts. This approach is embedded within the consortium, leveraging synergies among actors and complementary interventions to address immediate needs while laying the groundwork for sustainable solutions.

Building on previous cycles of this project, BTF6 also leverages synergies with existing initiatives of consortium members to maximise impact and create sustainable solutions. AVSI has for example established frameworks for multi-sectoral support in Lebanon resulting in access to art therapy services and strengthened public school capacities to facilitate referrals, while Terre des Hommes contributes synergies by its focus on retention, digitalisation, and accessibility. Plan International's existing programs focus on education, but also include humanitarian components such as MPCA, food assistance, and protection services. These programs foster social cohesion, support vulnerable families, and provide direct assistance to Syrian refugees and host communities. Coordination among members of the consortium ensures the integration of initiatives. By building on lessons learned, the consortium enhances community cohesion, strengthens public structures, and promotes inclusive economic opportunities, in an approach that ensures ongoing efforts foster a comprehensive response that addresses immediate education and protection needs, builds resilience, and supports sustainable solutions for vulnerable refugee communities.

For Early Childhood Education (ECE), the BTF consortium will target children aged 5 to ensure the early childhood development of necessary skills that will allow needed social, emotional and academic preparation of children to access formal education in Prep-ECE and grade 1. Although completion of ECE level 3 does not currently constitute a pre-requisite for enrollment in formal education (FE), the Consortium has gathered consistent insights on the determinant positive impact of prior engagement in learning. Through ECE, children are offered the opportunity to develop fundamental social and inter-personal skills and to receive specialized support to address special needs, building the foundations for more effective transition and retention in FE.
For Basic Literacy and Numeracy (BLN), the BTF consortium will target children aged 8 to 14 with no prior learning or who have been out of school for two years or longer, in line with standard operating procedures of respective line ministries. This target group is currently excluded from accessing formal education. Although a comprehensive transition framework has until date not been consolidated, the government is committed to issuing a reform of transition pathways by Summer 2025. The Consortium will offer the three levels of the BLN program, ensuring completion of level 3 by the end of the action. To sustain efforts towards attainment of learning outcomes, the Consortium has integrated, as of BTF5, a remedial component, to provide tailored support to those students who at the end of the cycle have not achieved the learning objectives of their respective level. In this way, children are effectively supported in completing the cycle successfully and transition to the subsequent level – and eventually to formal education.
All non-formal education (NFE) activities will be supplemented with highly engaging and interactive activities, to stimulate the interest and commitment of the children to learning. Additionally, NFE programs are complemented by an integrated package of age-appropriate psychosocial support (PSS), with Social-emotional learning embedded in the ECE curriculum, and Life Skills in BLN. This latter component will be facilitated by dedicated staff with adequate professional qualifications, supporting the development of needed skills, all the while facilitating the safe identification and referral of children exposed to child protection risks. This will also be enhanced through provision of capacity building and training of all frontliners, including teachers and education personnel.
Aiming to strengthen the quality of teaching and learning, the Consortium will target teachers and education personnel with capacity development opportunities, with the twofold objective of increasing knowledge and teaching skills to address children’s learning needs and providing psycho-social support in the form of self-care. This is in line with the Consortium’s approach to integrating Child Protection in NFE, enhancing the protective dimension of education services.
Grounding on the socio-ecological model and with a view to further strengthening the broader safety and protection environment for children, affecting educational outcomes, the action integrates a Protection component. For children identified at medium/high risk of CP violations, the Consortium will provide direct case management services ensuring timely and effective response to urgent needs. Qualified case workers will be shadowing the implementation of NFE activities and attend the learning centers, providing an opportunity for children and caregivers to familiarize themselves with the CP staff, be informed of service availability, and build trust for disclosures and case management. Case management processes will be aimed at reducing the CP risk, through the accompaniment of the child and their trusted adult. Case management will be provided in line with national SoPs, ensuring referral to relevant pathways and services. To mitigate the risk of negative coping mechanisms, including, but not limited to, child labour, identified risks will also be tackled through provision of Cash Assistance.
Acknowledging the pivotal contribution of positive parenting to children’s emotional and cognitive development, the Consortium will target caregivers through psycho-social support tackling self-care, ability to cope and social connectedness. By enhancing caregivers’ wellbeing, the action enhances support networks for children at the household level, with a positive return on children’s own wellbeing.
Gender, age, and disability inclusion will be mainstreamed throughout the action, to cater for the needs of vulnerable groups with adaptive response. It is noteworthy that children identified with disabilities and learning difficulties will be further supported through provision of specialized services and assistive devices.

SUMMARY Back to the Future is an ECHO-funded project in Lebanon led by AVSI and currently on the 6th iteration (BTF6), which Plan International has joined as a co-partner. BTF6 mainly targets vulnerable out-of-school Syrian refugee girls and boys in underserved locations with non-formal education programs complemented by psychosocial support. This includes basic literacy and numeracy for children aged 8 to 14 who have been out of school for two years or longer, and community-based early childhood education that aims to prepare children in their final year before school to transition to formal education for children aged 5. Plan’s role will be to implement BTF6 in Bekaa and Akkar, covering education in emergencies and child protection in emergencies activities almost entirely through local partner Human Aid and Development (HAND).

Since 2019, Lebanon has faced a crisis marked by economic collapse, political instability and social unrest. These challenges worsened after the outbreak of war in 2023, especially affecting marginalised groups like Syrian refugees. Even before the conflict, around 1.3 million children needed help accessing education, with Syrian refugee children being the most excluded. School disruptions caused by war left most Syrian children out of school. Barriers include unaffordable school costs, lack of transportation, limited school capacity, and systemic issues like child labor and legal documentation problems. Many children have no access to formal education due to stalled reforms. Unique needs of children like different language or disabilities in combination with untrained teachers further increase dropout rates. On top of these educational challenges, children face increased risks of abuse, neglect, and exploitation. Emotional and physical abuse is widespread, often linked to caregivers’ mental health struggles. The combination of economic hardship, displacement, systemic failures and social discrimination create a cycle of vulnerability, pushing refugee families and children into harmful coping strategies and deepening inequality.

The goal of Back to the Future VI is to ensure that vulnerable girls and boys in marginalized communities in Lebanon have access to inclusive quality education. The project ensures the provision of educational opportunities for out-of-school children at the community level through non-formal education programs. Moreover, the project provides a protective environment and supports the wellbeing of children and their families to support their engagement in educational activities.

This project primarily targets vulnerable out-of-school Syrian refugee girls and boys in underserved locations. Efforts to enhance Basic Literacy and Numeracy (BLN) skills are envisaged to reach children aged 8 to 14 who have been out of school for two years or longer specifically, while Community-Based Early Childhood Education is organised for children aged 5.

title.narrative: Protective education services
Number of teachers and other education personnel showing an increased knowledge on relevant protection subjects

description.narrative: Other education personnel may include supporting mechanisms such as parents-teachers associations, mothers-students associations, and school management associations. Protection needs to be defined for the project based on identified contextual hazards, risks and vulnerabilities (e.g. child protection, psycho-social support, SGBV information, Mine/UXO risk education, HIV/AIDS, nutrition, health and hygiene, gender sensitive education, PSS and SEL and conflict sensitive education). Disaggregation of data by sex, NFE type or level of education (primary, lower secondary, upper secondary) and disability to be provided.

title.narrative: Quality teaching and learning
Number of girls and boys provided essential learning materials for basic education

description.narrative: The minimum package of learning materials to be defined by partners based on the project focus. This should ensure that basic supplies of textbooks (or equivalent), reading materials and stationery are available to learners. Learning materials to include adaptations and modifications for learners living with disabilities where needed, and tailored to the language needs identified. Where learning kits are provided per classroom, a breakdown of content must be provided to justify reasonable provision per child. Materials may be supplied directly by the project or support (logistical/technical/advocacy/other) may be provided to education authorities to facilitate provision. Disaggregation of data by sex, NFE type or level of education (primary, lower secondary, upper secondary) and disability to be provided.
